title: Warsh's 'Dose of Accommodation' Remark Has Wall Street Bracing for More Fed Rate Hikes
excerpt: The Fed chairman's deliberate phrasing after September's rate hike — the first in three years — has traders, banks and economists debating how many more increases are coming.
body:
• Fed Chair Kevin Warsh described the September rate hike as removing "a dose of accommodation" — a phrase he repeated several times, signaling more tightening may follow.
  • Goldman Sachs and Bank of America both added an October rate hike to their forecasts; CME FedWatch put the odds of an October move at 58%, up from 42% a week earlier.
  • Futures markets are pricing a fed funds rate near 4.635% by the end of 2027, implying three or four more hikes ahead.
  • For borrowers, the cost is already rising: the 10-year Treasury yield hit 5.223%, its highest since June 2007, and the 30-year bond reached 5.501%, the highest since 2004. Mortgage rates move with the 10-year yield, so homebuyers should expect higher monthly payments as long as the Fed keeps hiking.

Three words from Kevin Warsh have upended Wall Street's thinking about the Federal Reserve's path forward. At his press conference following the central bank's September 15-16 meeting — which raised the benchmark rate a quarter point to 3.75%-4%, the first increase in more than three years — the Fed chairman did not frame the move as a simple tightening. He described it as removing "a dose of accommodation."

The wording may sound like central-bank semantics. Markets heard something else: an opening bid. Krishna Guha, head of economics and central bank strategy at Evercore ISI, called the phrase "the one stand-out hawkish element" of Warsh's commentary. "This was not a mistake; it was a phrase he repeated several times and looked very much a deliberate choice to frame policy in this way," Guha wrote in a client note, adding that the framing "raises the possibility of a more open-ended approach to the number of hikes that might be required."

"Warsh's framing, if taken literally, raises the possibility that rates might have to keep going up until financial conditions facing the private sector are no longer 'accommodative' — however that is defined. This is a relatively open-ended prospect."

— Krishna Guha, Evercore ISI

From insurance cuts to an open-ended campaign

The September decision itself was widely expected. The Federal Open Market Committee voted 12-0 to lift the federal funds target range from 3.5%-3.75% to 3.75%-4%, a move futures markets had priced at more than 90% odds heading into the meeting, according to the CME FedWatch tool. In their new economic projections, officials penciled in one more hike by year-end.

What caught traders off guard was the posture. The phrase "dose of accommodation" implies the Fed believes its policy stance is still stimulative — meaning this hike is the first of several steps to withdraw support it no longer considers necessary. "The word 'accommodation' means 'stimulus' at the Fed; this comment implies that the current monetary policy stance is meaningfully stimulative," wrote James Egelhof, chief U.S. economist at BNP Paribas Securities. With policy starting from a stimulative stance, a strong cyclical impulse and persistent inflation, he argued, "significant rate increases, perhaps more than the three we expect, may be necessary."

Warsh refused to anchor the discussion to the neutral rate — the level at which policy neither boosts nor restrains growth — a framework central banks have used for more than a decade. Asked by CNBC's Steve Liesman how far the current rate sits above neutral, Warsh replied that measuring the benchmark relative to neutral is "useful academically" but has no "operational effect" on the decisions policymakers make today. The answer deepened his reputation for being cryptic about how he tunes policy.

Wall Street reprices the path

The speculation began immediately. Goldman Sachs and Bank of America both added an October increase to their forecasts, and Bank of America expects another move in December as well. Market-implied odds of an October hike stood near 58% on Friday morning, up from 42% a week earlier, per CME Group's FedWatch gauge. Futures contracts imply a fed funds rate of about 4.635% near the end of 2027 — three or four more hikes from here.

Not everyone buys the hawkish read. "We remain unconvinced that this is the start of an aggressive new tightening cycle," said Jack Janasiewicz, portfolio manager and lead portfolio strategist at Natixis Investment Managers Solutions. "Rather, we see this as a removal of the insurance cuts the Fed delivered in the fall of 2025" under Warsh's predecessor, Jerome Powell — who now sits on the committee as a governor.

What it means for borrowers and investors

Bond markets have already moved. The 10-year Treasury yield surged more than 10 basis points to 5.223%, a level CNBC reported had not been reached since June 2007, driven by stubborn inflation, rising energy prices and heavy debt issuance tied to the AI data-center buildout. The 30-year bond yield rose to 5.501%, its highest since 2004, while the 2-year yield — the most sensitive to near-term Fed policy — climbed to 4.941%.

For homebuyers and mortgage holders, that matters directly. Thirty-year fixed mortgage rates track the 10-year Treasury yield, so every additional hike the Fed delivers keeps borrowing costs elevated or pushes them higher. Borrowers considering refinancing or buying in the coming months face a market where rates are unlikely to fall back toward the levels of recent years. On the other side of the ledger, savers continue to benefit: higher policy rates have kept yields on money-market funds and short-term CDs elevated.

For Indian diaspora homebuyers in the U.S., the math is unforgiving — a higher 10-year yield translates almost directly into higher monthly mortgage payments, making lock-in timing and down-payment size more consequential than at any point in nearly two decades.

What to watch next

The Fed meets again in October, and the new forecasts already bake in another hike by year-end. Warsh has refused to submit economic projections or offer forward guidance, so markets will parse every press conference for the kind of deliberate phrasing that moved them this time. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has voiced confidence in Warsh, while President Donald Trump — who appointed him after demanding rate cuts — has directed his criticism at the Fed board rather than its chairman. The question for the next meeting: whether "a dose" was the start of a prescription.
